subtopic_detail: Persistent head tilt in an eight week old with a firm sternocleidomastoid swelling and full eye movements
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing an 8 week old boy whose mother says he has always held his head over to the right and only looks to his left when she feeds him. He was born at term by forceps delivery after a long second stage, and she has noticed the back of his head is becoming flat on the right.

He feeds and settles normally and is gaining weight along the 50th centile. On examination there is a firm painless swelling within the right sternocleidomastoid. He follows your face smoothly to both sides through a full range of eye movement, and the red reflex is present and symmetrical.

data_table.Examination: Head tilted towards the right shoulder with the chin turned to the left, firm 1.5 cm swelling within the lower right sternocleidomastoid, passive rotation of the head to the right limited to about 45 degrees, passive left lateral flexion limited, right occipital flattening, full and equal eye movements with symmetrical red reflexes, tone and reflexes normal in all four limbs, hips abduct fully with no clunk

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Request an ultrasound of the neck swelling before any other management
options.rationale: Ultrasound is reserved for a mass with atypical features such as rapid growth, a location outside the muscle belly, or overlying skin change, none of which are present. Imaging a typical muscular mass delays the stretching programme, which is most effective in the first few months. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

options.text: Refer to a paediatric physiotherapist for stretching and positioning
options.rationale: A firm mass within the sternocleidomastoid with restricted passive rotation away from the tilt is the classic picture, and graded passive stretching with positioning to encourage active rotation resolves the great majority when started before six months. Referral is made on the clinical findings alone. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

options.text: Request a cervical spine radiograph series to exclude a bony anomaly
options.rationale: Bony torticollis from a hemivertebra or an atlantoaxial anomaly gives a fixed tilt without a palpable muscle mass, and passive correction is blocked rather than merely restricted. The near pair here is that muscular restriction yields partially to gentle pressure while bony restriction does not. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Torticollis in children)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Torticollis in children

options.text: Refer to a paediatric ophthalmologist for assessment of ocular alignment
options.rationale: Ocular torticollis from a superior oblique palsy produces a compensatory head posture with a normal neck on palpation and full passive movement. Smooth conjugate tracking through a full range and a symmetrical red reflex here argue against an ocular cause. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Torticollis in children)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Torticollis in children

options.text: Refer for a moulding helmet to correct the flattening of the occiput
options.rationale: The occipital flattening is secondary to the fixed head position, so treating the skull without treating the neck leaves the cause in place. Helmet therapy is considered only for severe residual deformity after the torticollis has been treated and repositioning has failed. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

explanation.summary: Congenital muscular torticollis affects up to one in 250 infants and is associated with instrumental delivery, breech presentation and a crowded intrauterine position. The head tilts towards the shortened muscle and the chin rotates away from it, so a right sided lesion gives a right tilt with the chin to the left. Positional plagiocephaly follows because the infant lies consistently on one side of the occiput, and developmental dysplasia of the hip is found in a small but real proportion, so the hips must be examined at the same visit. Physiotherapy started before six months resolves most cases without surgery, while presentations left beyond one year increasingly need surgical release.
key_points: The head tilts towards the tight muscle and the chin turns away from it
A palpable mass within the sternocleidomastoid supports a muscular cause
Full passive eye movement argues against a compensatory ocular head posture
Examine the hips, since dysplasia coexists in a minority of infants
Plagiocephaly is secondary and resolves as the neck posture corrects
explanation.pearls: Failure of the head tilt to improve after six weeks of physiotherapy, or the appearance of a tilt after four months of age in a previously straight infant, should prompt imaging for a posterior fossa tumour rather than a further course of stretching.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Torticollis in children

subtopic_detail: Persistent single joint swelling in a preschool girl with a positive antinuclear antibody and no eye symptoms
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 3 year old girl whose left knee has been swollen for ten weeks. Her mother says she is stiff and limping when she first gets up, and by lunchtime she is running about normally.

There has been no injury, no fever and no rash, and she has grown along the 75th centile throughout. Her eyes look normal to her parents and she has never complained of pain or blurring in them. Examination shows a warm knee with an effusion and a 10 degree loss of full extension, with no other joint involved.

data_table.Examination: Left knee warm with a moderate effusion, fixed flexion of 10 degrees, no erythema, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, no rash, remaining joints and spine normal, eyes white with normal pupils on external inspection
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 121 g/L (110-140), white cell count 8.4 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), platelets 342 x10^9/L (150-450), C reactive protein 6 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 24 mm/h (less than 15), antinuclear antibody positive at 1:320, blood culture negative

lead_in: Which additional step is most important to arrange now?

options.text: Arrange joint aspiration and start intravenous flucloxacillin empirically
options.rationale: Septic arthritis presents over days with fever, refusal to weight bear and markedly raised inflammatory markers, not with ten weeks of morning stiffness that eases through the day. The inflammatory markers here are barely above range and she is systemically well. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute joint pain or swelling)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute joint pain or swelling

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the knee under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: Imaging is useful when a single joint problem might be mechanical or infective, but the diagnosis here rests on the duration and the pattern rather than on the appearance of the synovium. It also carries an anaesthetic that does nothing to protect her sight. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

options.text: Arrange a bone marrow aspirate before any corticosteroid is prescribed
options.rationale: Marrow examination is indicated when leukaemia is in the differential, flagged by night pain waking the child, cytopenias, or markedly raised lactate dehydrogenase with a low or normal white cell count. Her counts are normal and her pain eases with movement, which is the opposite of the malignant pattern. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

options.text: Arrange slit lamp examination by an ophthalmologist within the month
options.rationale: Chronic anterior uveitis in this pattern of arthritis is silent, produces no redness or pain, and is detected only on slit lamp examination, yet untreated it causes synechiae, cataract and visual loss. Young age at onset with a positive antinuclear antibody carries the highest risk, warranting screening three monthly. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

options.text: Arrange serial antistreptolysin O titres and an echocardiogram this week
options.rationale: Post streptococcal and rheumatic joint disease is migratory, painful out of proportion to the swelling and follows a documented throat or skin infection within weeks. A single joint swollen continuously for ten weeks does not fit that timeline. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute joint pain or swelling)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute joint pain or swelling

explanation.summary: Oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis is the commonest form in Australian children and typically presents in girls under six with one or two large joints swollen for more than six weeks. Pain is often unimpressive and the child compensates with a limp that improves as the day goes on, which is why the diagnosis is frequently delayed. The eye complication is the reason the diagnosis matters urgently, because the inflammation is asymptomatic and the child is far too young to report visual change. Treatment of the joint itself usually begins with intra-articular corticosteroid, with methotrexate added for persistent or extending disease.
key_points: Arthritis is defined by six weeks or more of joint swelling or restriction
Morning stiffness that eases with activity separates it from mechanical pain
Antinuclear antibody positivity raises uveitis risk, not diagnostic certainty
Uveitis is silent, so screening is by slit lamp rather than by symptoms
Intra-articular corticosteroid is the usual first treatment for a single joint
explanation.pearls: A child under seven at onset with a positive antinuclear antibody needs slit lamp screening every three months for the first four years, whereas an older antibody negative child can be screened every six to twelve months.

sources.label: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis
RCH CPG: Acute joint pain or swelling
BMJ Best Practice: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

subtopic_detail: Preschool boy with late walking, bulky calves and a positive Gowers manoeuvre with preserved reflexes
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general clinic seeing a 4 year old boy referred because he cannot keep up with other children. His mother says he first walked at 19 months, takes the stairs one foot at a time holding the rail, and gets up off the carpet by pushing on his own thighs with his hands.

He has about 50 words of speech and is otherwise well, with no regression of skills. His calves look bulky and feel firm. Deep tendon reflexes are present at the knees and ankles, tone is normal and there is no clonus, and his gait is waddling with no foot drop.

data_table.Examination: Waddling gait, rises from the floor by climbing up his legs with his hands, hip girdle weakness with power 4 out of 5, shoulder girdle power 5 out of 5, calves firm and enlarged bilaterally, knee and ankle reflexes present and symmetrical, plantar responses flexor, no sensory level, spine straight with no hairy patch or dimple

lead_in: Which investigation should be performed first?

options.text: Nerve conduction studies with electromyography under sedation
options.rationale: Neurophysiology localises a neuropathic process, which typically gives distal weakness, absent reflexes and sensory change. Reflexes are preserved and the weakness is proximal here, and the test is invasive in a preschooler when a blood test answers the question. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine with contrast
options.rationale: Spinal imaging is for a cord lesion or tethering, signalled by upper motor neurone signs, a sensory level, bladder change or a midline cutaneous marker. None are present and his plantar responses are flexor. (Source: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness

options.text: Serum creatine kinase measured before any other investigation
options.rationale: Proximal weakness with calf hypertrophy and a positive Gowers manoeuvre is a muscular pattern, and creatine kinase is elevated ten to a hundred times the upper limit in dystrophinopathy, making it the cheap decisive first test. A normal result effectively excludes the diagnosis and redirects the work up. (Source: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness

options.text: Referral to physiotherapy for gait retraining and review in six months
options.rationale: Physiotherapy is part of long term care but delaying the diagnosis by six months costs the family genetic counselling and delays corticosteroid treatment that preserves ambulation. Weakness with calf hypertrophy is never a normal variant of gait. (Source: Australian Institute of Musculoskeletal Science: Neuromuscular disorders in children)
source_refs: Australian Institute of Musculoskeletal Science: Neuromuscular disorders in children

options.text: Open muscle biopsy of the vastus lateralis arranged this month
options.rationale: Biopsy was the historical confirmatory test but has been displaced by genetic analysis of the dystrophin gene, which is performed after the creatine kinase result rather than instead of it. It is reserved for the child with a high creatine kinase whose genetic testing is uninformative. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

explanation.summary: Dystrophinopathy affects about one in 5000 boys and the average age at diagnosis remains close to five years despite the signs usually being present by three. Late walking, a waddling gait, difficulty with stairs and calf hypertrophy are the recognisable cluster, and mild global developmental delay including speech delay accompanies it in roughly a third because dystrophin is expressed in brain. The diagnostic sequence is creatine kinase first, then genetic testing of the dystrophin gene, with biopsy reserved for unresolved cases. Early diagnosis matters because corticosteroids prolong independent walking, cardiac surveillance begins in childhood, and the mother and her sisters need carrier testing.
key_points: Proximal weakness with preserved reflexes points to muscle, not nerve
A positive Gowers manoeuvre signals hip girdle rather than distal weakness
Creatine kinase is the decisive first test and is grossly elevated
Genetic testing of the dystrophin gene confirms the diagnosis
Speech delay coexists in a substantial minority and is not a separate problem
explanation.pearls: Any boy not walking independently by 18 months, or any child with an unexplained transaminase rise on routine bloods, should have a creatine kinase measured, because a raised alanine aminotransferase of muscle origin is a common accidental route to the diagnosis.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness
BMJ Best Practice: Duchenne muscular dystrophy
Australian Institute of Musculoskeletal Science: Neuromuscular disorders in children

subtopic_detail: Habitual snoring with witnessed pauses in a healthy five year old with large tonsils and normal growth
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 5 year old girl whose parents say she snores loudly every night and sleeps with her mouth open and her neck arched back. Twice a week her father has watched her stop breathing for several seconds before she gasps and starts again.

Her kindergarten teacher has raised concerns about inattention and afternoon irritability, and she still naps most days. She was born at term, has no asthma, no allergic rhinitis and no syndromic features, and she is growing along the 50th centile for height and weight. Her tonsils meet close to the midline and her nasal airway is narrow.

data_table.Examination: Tonsils enlarged to grade 3 bilaterally with no exudate, hyponasal voice, mouth breathing at rest, nasal mucosa pink with no polyps or allergic crease, tympanic membranes normal, chest clear with no chest wall deformity, cardiovascular examination normal, body mass index on the 55th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Refer to an otolaryngologist for consideration of adenotonsillectomy
options.rationale: An otherwise healthy child between two and twelve with habitual snoring, witnessed apnoeas and adenotonsillar hypertrophy can be referred for surgery on clinical grounds, and removal of the obstructing tissue is the definitive treatment with documented gains in behaviour and quality of life. (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive sleep apnoea)

options.text: Arrange overnight polysomnography before any referral is made
options.rationale: Formal sleep study is reserved for children under two, those with obesity, craniofacial or neuromuscular disease or Down syndrome, and cases where the history and the airway findings disagree. Insisting on it for a straightforward presentation adds months of waiting without changing the decision. (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive sleep apnoea)

options.text: Start an intranasal corticosteroid spray and review her in three months
options.rationale: Intranasal corticosteroid helps mild snoring driven by allergic rhinitis, and the near pair here is that rhinitis gives a pale boggy mucosa, an allergic crease and seasonal symptoms. Her mucosa is normal and she has witnessed apnoeas, which is beyond the reach of a nasal spray. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: Provide sleep hygiene advice with a bedtime routine and review in a month
options.rationale: Behavioural sleep advice addresses settling difficulty and night waking, not an obstructed upper airway. A child who stops breathing in her sleep is not having a behavioural problem and the delay allows the daytime consequences to continue. (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive sleep apnoea)

options.text: Refer to a paediatrician for assessment of attention and behaviour first
options.rationale: Inattention here is a consequence of fragmented sleep, and assessing it before the airway risks a stimulant prescription for a reversible problem. Behavioural referral is appropriate if the symptoms persist once the obstruction has been treated. (Source: Australian Sleep Association: Paediatric sleep disordered breathing)
source_refs: Australian Sleep Association: Paediatric sleep disordered breathing

explanation.summary: Obstructive sleep apnoea affects between one and four per cent of Australian children and peaks between two and eight years when the tonsils and adenoids are largest relative to the airway. The presentation differs from adults, with daytime hyperactivity, inattention and irritability rather than sleepiness, so it is frequently mistaken for a primary behavioural disorder. Untreated disease causes growth faltering, learning difficulty, enuresis and in severe cases pulmonary hypertension. In the otherwise healthy preschool or school aged child, the Australian pathway accepts a clinical diagnosis and refers for adenotonsillectomy without waiting for a sleep study.
key_points: Habitual snoring with witnessed apnoeas is the core clinical picture
Daytime inattention rather than sleepiness is the childhood presentation
Polysomnography is for under twos, comorbidity, or a discordant history
Adenotonsillectomy is the definitive treatment for adenotonsillar disease
Untreated disease can cause growth faltering and pulmonary hypertension
explanation.pearls: A child under three years, or one with an oxygen saturation nadir below 80 per cent on any sleep study, should have the surgery performed in a centre with paediatric intensive care access because of the risk of postoperative respiratory compromise in the first night.

sources.label: Australian Sleep Association: Paediatric sleep disordered breathing

subtopic_detail: Fourteen months of waxing and waning blinking and throat clearing in a school aged boy with no functional impairment
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 9 year old boy whose parents are worried about repeated hard blinking and a throat clearing noise that has been present on and off for 14 months. The movements come in runs for a few weeks, settle for a while, then return, and are worse when he is tired or excited before a football match.

He can hold them back for a minute or two when he concentrates, and then they come out in a burst. His teacher has not raised any concern, his marks are good and he has friends. He is not distressed by the movements himself, and his neurological examination is normal.

data_table.Examination: Frequent brief forceful eye blinking and intermittent throat clearing during the consultation, movements suppressible on request for about 90 seconds, no impairment of conscious state during the movements, cranial nerves normal, tone power and coordination normal, no chorea, gait normal, conjunctivae white with no discharge

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start risperidone at a low dose and review the response in six weeks
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are reserved for tics causing pain, injury or significant social or educational impairment, none of which apply, and they carry weight gain, sedation and prolactin elevation in a growing child. Treating a well functioning child exposes him to harm for no measurable gain. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Start clonidine at night and titrate the dose over the next six weeks
options.rationale: Clonidine is a reasonable first pharmacological choice when tics do warrant treatment, particularly with coexisting attention difficulties, so the near pair question is whether any drug is indicated at all. Here the threshold of impairment has not been crossed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange an electroencephalogram to characterise the repeated movements
options.rationale: Electroencephalography is for events with impaired awareness, automatisms or a stereotyped unvarying pattern, since seizures are neither suppressible nor responsive to distraction. His movements can be held back voluntarily, which is not a feature of epilepsy. (Source: RCH CPG: Tics)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and measure copper studies
options.rationale: Imaging and copper studies belong to the child with a progressive movement disorder, dystonia, cognitive decline or abnormal neurological signs. A normal examination with a fluctuating fourteen month course is characteristic of a primary tic disorder. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Tic disorders)

options.text: Explain the natural history and arrange planned review in six months
options.rationale: A combination of motor and vocal tics for more than a year that waxes and wanes is expected to peak around ten to twelve years and then improve through adolescence, and when there is no functional impairment the evidence supports education and monitoring rather than drug treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Tics)

explanation.summary: Tics affect up to one in five school aged children at some point and the combination of multiple motor tics with at least one vocal tic for over a year defines the syndrome that carries Gilles de la Tourette's name. The defining features are a premonitory urge, brief voluntary suppressibility followed by a rebound, and a fluctuating course that typically worsens with fatigue, excitement or illness. Severity peaks around puberty and improves substantially in most by the late teens, which is why the first intervention is accurate information for the child, the family and the school. Comorbid attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and obsessive compulsive symptoms cause more impairment than the tics themselves and should be actively sought.
key_points: Suppressibility with rebound distinguishes tics from seizures and chorea
Motor plus vocal tics for over twelve months defines the syndrome
Waxing and waning severity with stress and fatigue is expected
Education and monitoring are first line when function is preserved
Screen for attention and obsessive compulsive symptoms at every review
explanation.pearls: Comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics, built around habit reversal training, is the recommended first active treatment when impairment does appear, and it outperforms medication for tic severity without the metabolic cost of an antipsychotic.

subtopic_detail: Four months of bilateral evening leg pain in a well six year old who runs normally by day with a normal examination
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6 year old girl who has been waking in the evening crying with pain in both calves and the fronts of both thighs, three or four nights a week for four months. Her mother rubs her legs and she settles within twenty minutes and sleeps through the rest of the night.

She is up and running at school the next morning with no limp and has not missed a day. There is no fever, no weight loss, no night sweats and no bruising, and she plays netball each weekend. Her aunt has juvenile arthritis and her mother is anxious about that. Examination of both legs is entirely normal.

data_table.Examination: Height and weight tracking along the 60th centile, no pallor, no bruising or petechiae, no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly, no bone tenderness over the tibiae femora or spine, hips and knees with full painless range of movement, no joint swelling or warmth, normal gait and normal single leg hop on each side

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange a full blood count with a blood film and measure lactate dehydrogenase
options.rationale: Blood testing is indicated when pain wakes the child from established sleep, is unilateral or localised to bone, or comes with pallor, bruising, fever or weight loss. None of those are present and her daytime function is unaffected. (Source: RCH CPG: Growing pains)

options.text: Explain the pattern, advise simple analgesia and review if features change
options.rationale: Bilateral pain confined to the evening with complete freedom of movement and a normal examination the following day is the recognised benign pattern, and positive diagnosis with safety netting avoids a cascade of tests. The parents are told exactly which changes would prompt reassessment. (Source: RCH CPG: Growing pains)

options.text: Arrange radiographs of both femora and both tibiae to exclude a bony lesion
options.rationale: Radiographs are for focal bone tenderness, a palpable mass or a limp, since osteoid osteoma and osteosarcoma are localised rather than symmetrical. Symmetrical pain with no tenderness anywhere does not fit a structural lesion. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Limb pain in children)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Limb pain in children

options.text: Measure the serum 25 hydroxyvitamin D level and treat if it is below range
options.rationale: Vitamin D deficiency causes bone pain with proximal weakness, a waddling gait and sometimes deformity or fracture, and the near pair is that its pain persists through the day rather than resolving by morning. Testing without those features usually yields an incidental result that is then treated pointlessly. (Source: RACGP: Vitamin D testing)

options.text: Refer to a paediatric rheumatologist for assessment of inflammatory joint pain
options.rationale: Inflammatory joint disease shows morning stiffness with swelling or restricted movement of a specific joint, the opposite of the diurnal pattern here where mornings are her best time. The family history raises the possibility but her examination does not support it. (Source: RCH CPG: Growing pains)

explanation.summary: Benign nocturnal limb pain of childhood affects around a third of children between three and twelve years and is a positive diagnosis rather than a diagnosis of exclusion. The defining pattern is bilateral pain in the muscles of the legs, late in the day or in the evening, with the child entirely well and fully mobile between episodes and a normal examination. The features that move a child out of this category are pain that is unilateral, localised over bone, present in the morning, associated with limp, swelling, fever, weight loss or systemic upset, or that wakes the child repeatedly from deep sleep. Massage, stretching and simple analgesia are effective, and the condition resolves over months to a few years.
key_points: The pain is bilateral and muscular rather than over a specific bone
Symptoms appear in the evening and the child is well the next morning
Examination must be entirely normal to make the diagnosis
Limp, morning symptoms or systemic features demand investigation
Massage and simple analgesia with parental reassurance are sufficient
explanation.pearls: Pain that is reliably worst in the morning, or that has been present for weeks over a single bony point, should prompt a full blood count with film and a plain radiograph of that bone, because leukaemia can present with normal peripheral counts in about one in ten children.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Limb pain in children
